newsitem.title: USA: Castle Rock wins Seinfeld copyright ruling.
newsitem.headline: Castle Rock wins Seinfeld copyright ruling.

text.p: The producer of the "Seinfeld" comedy series saw no humour in a book of trivia questions about the show and won a copyright infringement ruling against its publisher, according to court papers made public on Friday.

U.S. District Judge Sonia Sotomayor, in a ruling dated Thursday, granted producer Castle Rock Entertainment's motion for a summary judgment against Carol Publishing Group for wrongfully using original material from the highly successful programme.
A summary judgment is a ruling on the merits of a case without its going to trial.
However, Sotomayor did not grant Castle Rock's summary judgment motion for a claim of unfair competition, and that matter may proceed to trial.

The book, "The Seinfeld Aptitude Test" (SAT), contains 643 trivia questions about the events and characters on the Seinfeld show. It draws from 84 of the 86 Seinfeld episodes that had been broadcast at the time the book was published in 1994.

Its author, Beth Golub, said in court papers that the Emmy-awarding winning programme, which airs on NBC, is "about absolutely nothing" and the book "like the Seinfeld show, is devoted to the trifling, picayune and petty annoyances encountered by the show's characters on a daily basis."

Castle Rock argued that SAT was produced without its cooperation or approval and that it plans to pursue an aggressive marketing strategy that will include books related to the programme. It has already licensed the production of a CD-ROM product that includes discussions of Seinfeld episodes and which might ultimately include a trivia bank.
Carol Publishing argued that SAT did not misuse information that is protected by Castle Rock's copyright, but merely quizzes readers about the show's underlying facts and ideas.
But the judge found that the publisher had wrongfully copied original elements of the Seinfeld show.

"The facts revealed during an episode of Seinfeld are created by the show's writers. Thus, by reporting 'facts' from each episode .... defendants have appropriated 'original components' of plaintiff's protected work," she said.
"SAT seizes upon the notion which lies at the very heart of Seinfeld -- that there is humour in the mundane, seemingly trivial aspects of everyday life."

She said that by inviting readers to recall literally 643 bits of information from various Seinfeld episodes, SAT follows the basic premise of the Seinfeld show by focusing on "minutiae in the day-to-day lives of the show's characters."
The judge said that not only does SAT draw upon significant elements of the Seinfeld programme, but it introduces relatively little additional material to the mix.
"Simply put, without Seinfeld, there can be no SAT," she said.
